reason: The hypothesis cites no prior evidence, and all key premises—linking Mo content to electronegativity-driven plasticity reduction, the effect of V substitution on bonding heterogeneity and dislocation motion, and the specific strength/plasticity values—are presented without any supporting references. Standard textbook knowledge does not cover these specific alloy-specific claims.
premises: High Mo content in equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo increases electronegativity difference and reduces plasticity
Reducing electronegativity difference promotes more uniform dislocation motion and increases plasticity
V has a high melting point and similar atomic size to Mo, helping retain solid solution strengthening
Partial substitution of Mo with V reduces overall electronegativity mismatch without causing phase instability up to ~30% substitution
The baseline alloy has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of ~1719 MPa and limited plasticity
